chapters.title: The world between the wars and after

points.title: The Treaty of Versailles
points.brief: The 1919 peace treaty blamed Germany for the First World War, took its land and colonies, cut its army and made it pay reparations, leaving deep resentment.

points.title: The Great Depression in Australia
points.brief: After the 1929 Wall Street crash, prices for Australia's exports fell and loans dried up. By 1932 nearly a third of Australian workers had no job.

points.title: The rise of fascism
points.brief: Fascist leaders such as Mussolini in Italy and Hitler in Germany used fear, nationalism and propaganda to win power, then crushed opposition and built up their armies.

points.title: The Cold War
points.brief: After 1945 the United States and the Soviet Union, with their allies, competed for power and influence without fighting each other directly, until the Soviet Union broke up in 1991.

points.title: Oral history as evidence
points.brief: Recorded interviews with people who lived through events give personal detail missing elsewhere, but memories fade and change, so they are checked against other sources.

points.title: Synthesising several sources
points.brief: Synthesising means combining evidence from several sources into one explanation, showing where they agree, where they differ and why.

points.title: Judging a historian's argument
points.brief: Weigh a historian's interpretation by the evidence it uses, what it leaves out, when it was written and what questions or values shaped it.

chapters.title: Causes and course of the war

points.title: Causes of the Second World War
points.brief: Resentment of the Treaty of Versailles, the Depression, the aggression of Germany, Italy and Japan, and Britain and France's policy of appeasement all led to war.

points.title: The war begins in Europe
points.brief: Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939, and Australia joined Britain at war two days later. Blitzkrieg attacks conquered much of Europe by 1940.

points.title: The war in the Pacific
points.brief: Japan's attack on Pearl Harbor in December 1941 brought the United States into the war, and Japan swept south through South-East Asia towards Australia.

points.title: Turning points of the war
points.brief: Defeats at Midway and Stalingrad in 1942 and 1943 stopped Japan and Germany advancing, and the D-Day landings in 1944 opened a second front in western Europe.

points.title: The Holocaust
points.brief: Nazi Germany carried out the planned murder of about six million Jews, along with Roma, disabled people and others, in ghettos, mass shootings and death camps.

points.title: The atomic bombs and the end of the war
points.brief: The United States dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August 1945, and Japan surrendered days later. Historians still debate whether the bombs were needed.

chapters.title: Australians in the Second World War

points.title: The siege of Tobruk
points.brief: In 1941 Australian troops held the Libyan port of Tobruk against German and Italian forces for months, earning the name Rats of Tobruk.

points.title: The fall of Singapore and prisoners of war
points.brief: Singapore fell to Japan in February 1942 and about 15,000 Australians were captured. Thousands of prisoners died from starvation, disease and brutality, as on the Burma-Thailand Railway.

points.title: The bombing of Darwin
points.brief: On 19 February 1942 Japanese aircraft bombed Darwin, killing more than 230 people, the first of many raids on northern Australia.

points.title: The Kokoda Track
points.brief: In 1942 Australian soldiers, helped by Papuan carriers, fought the Japanese along the Kokoda Track in Papua and pushed them back from Port Moresby.

chapters.title: The home front and the war's legacy

points.title: Wartime government controls
points.brief: The government rationed food and clothing, directed people into war work, censored news and interned people seen as enemy aliens.

points.title: Women's changing roles in wartime
points.brief: Women joined the armed services and the Land Army and took jobs in factories once held by men, though usually for lower pay and only until the war ended.

points.title: First Nations Australians in the Second World War
points.brief: Thousands of First Nations Australians served, including in the Torres Strait Light Infantry Battalion, often for less pay and without equal rights at home.

points.title: Turning to the United States
points.brief: With Britain unable to defend it, Prime Minister Curtin said in 1941 that Australia looked to America. The ANZUS treaty of 1951 made the alliance formal.

points.title: Remembering the Second World War
points.brief: Anzac Day, memorials and the growth of Kokoda as a place of pilgrimage keep the war in memory, while historians debate what it means for Australian identity.

chapters.title: Post-war Australia and the Cold War

points.title: Populate or perish
points.brief: After the war, Arthur Calwell's immigration program brought in displaced people from Europe and then other migrants, to build the population and workforce.

points.title: The end of the White Australia policy
points.brief: The policy was eased from 1966 and ended in 1973. Multiculturalism followed, and refugees arrived from Vietnam after 1975.

points.title: Fear of communism in Australia
points.brief: In the Cold War, Prime Minister Menzies tried to ban the Communist Party, but voters rejected the change at a referendum in 1951.

points.title: The Vietnam War and conscription
points.brief: To stop the spread of communism, Australia sent military advisers to Vietnam from 1962 and combat troops from 1965, including young men conscripted by a birthday ballot.

points.title: The anti-war movement
points.brief: Opposition to conscription and the war grew into mass moratorium marches in 1970, and the last combat troops came home in the early 1970s.

points.title: Protection and assimilation
points.brief: Protection policies controlled First Nations Australians' lives. Assimilation, from the 1930s, expected them to give up their cultures and live like white Australians.

points.title: The Stolen Generations
points.brief: For much of the 20th century, governments and churches removed First Nations children from their families, causing harm that continues across generations.

points.title: The Day of Mourning
points.brief: On 26 January 1938, as others celebrated 150 years since the First Fleet, Aboriginal activists such as William Cooper, Jack Patten and William Ferguson met in Sydney to protest and demand equal rights.

points.title: The Freedom Ride
points.brief: In 1965 Charles Perkins led university students on a bus tour of New South Wales towns to expose racial segregation in pools, cinemas and shops.

points.title: The 1967 referendum
points.brief: Over 90 per cent voted to let the Commonwealth make laws for First Nations Australians and to count them in the census. It did not grant citizenship or the vote.

points.title: The Wave Hill walk-off
points.brief: In 1966 Vincent Lingiari led Gurindji workers off Wave Hill station over pay and conditions. Their strike became a claim for land, returned to them in 1975.

points.title: The Aboriginal Tent Embassy
points.brief: In 1972 activists set up a tent on the lawn of Parliament House in Canberra to demand land rights. It became a lasting symbol of protest.

points.title: Mabo and native title
points.brief: In 1992 the High Court ruled for Eddie Koiki Mabo and the Meriam people that native title had survived colonisation, rejecting terra nullius. The Native Title Act followed.

points.title: Bringing Them Home and the Apology
points.brief: The 1997 Bringing Them Home report told of the Stolen Generations, and in 2008 Prime Minister Rudd apologised to them on behalf of the nation.

chapters.title: Rights for women and for all

points.title: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights
points.brief: Adopted by the United Nations in 1948 after the war's horrors, it set out rights for every person. Australia's H. V. Evatt led the General Assembly that passed it.

points.title: The women's movement
points.brief: From the late 1960s, the women's liberation movement campaigned for equal rights in work, education, law and family life, and against discrimination.

points.title: Equal pay and the marriage bar
points.brief: Married women could keep federal public service jobs from 1966, and equal pay decisions in 1969 and 1972 set equal pay for work of equal value.

points.title: Anti-discrimination laws
points.brief: The Racial Discrimination Act of 1975 and the Sex Discrimination Act of 1984 made unfair treatment because of race or sex against the law.
